lesson.grammar_point: defining relative clauses: who (people), which / that (things), where (places); the relative pronoun can be omitted when it is the object

listenings.text: I was born in Amsterdam, and I love visitors, really. But let me give you some advice. The first thing that tourists do wrong is walking in the bike lanes. Please, look before you cross. Second, the center is beautiful, but it's not the only Amsterdam. Take the free ferry behind the central station. It goes to the north, an area where you find old factories that are now restaurants and galleries. And come in the autumn. It's the season when the city is quiet, and the light on the canals in the late afternoon is something you won't forget.

My first trip to Amsterdam was in August, and honestly, I didn't love it. It was crowded, it was hot, and the lines for the museums were incredibly long. So last year I went back, in October. What a difference. The streets were calm, the trees along the canals were yellow and red, and I could walk everywhere. The highlight of the trip was a small gallery that I found by accident. It belonged to an old woman who painted the canals every day. I bought one of her paintings, and it's on my wall now. Sometimes a city needs a second chance.

On my first day in Amsterdam, I rented a bike, and I was really nervous. There were bikes everywhere, and everybody was so fast. A woman who was waiting next to me at a red light saw my face and laughed. She taught me to use my hand to show where I was turning. It helped a lot. By the third day, I was riding like a local, well, almost. On the last day, I rode out of the city, along a river, to a village where there were windmills and cows. I would never see that on foot. If you go, rent a bike. Just stay in the bike lane.

reading.rtitle: Amsterdam in Autumn: A Short Guide
paras: Most tourists visit Amsterdam in the summer, when the streets are full and hotels are expensive. But many locals say the best season is the autumn. It is the time when the foliage along the canals turns yellow and red, the crowds go home, and the city becomes calm again. Bring a warm jacket, because it can be windy, and an umbrella, which you will probably need at least once.

Amsterdam is a city where almost everybody rides a bike, so the first rule is simple: never walk in a bike lane. The best way to see the city is to wander along the canals without a plan. You will see houseboats that people really live in, bridges that are hundreds of years old and small galleries that most tourists never find. If you want art, the big museums are open all year, but you should book in advance.

When it gets cold, do what the locals do: find a cozy café that has candles on the tables, and stay for hours. On Saturdays, visit a flea market where you can find old maps, books and vinyl records. And if you want to go off the beaten track, take the free ferry behind the central station to the north of the city, an area that most visitors never see.
